items.prompt: How many of White's legal moves give check in this position?

claims.statement: The bishop move to c4 gives check.
The knight move to e5 gives check.
These are all of White's legal moves.
After Ng5 the knight attacks f7.

hints: A check needs a white piece that can attack f7.
Look at the open diagonal from f1 and at the squares a knight on f3 can reach, including g5.
Three: the bishop to c4, and the knight to e5 or g5.
items.explain: The bishop on f1 reaches c4 and attacks f7 along an open diagonal. The knight on f3 reaches e5 and g5, and from either square it attacks f7. No other piece can check in one move, so there are three checks. One of them, Ng5+, loses the knight to the h6 pawn. Counting first tells Black exactly which replies must be ready.

items.prompt: Count the pieces defending the white pawn on d4. How many are there?

hints: Look for white pieces that see d4.

items.explain: The knight on f3 attacks d4, and the queen on d1 sees it along the open d-file. Nothing else defends it. Two defenders against two attackers means that a capture on d4 is not free for either side yet.

hints: Count each side separately.

items.explain: Black attacks d4 with the c5 pawn and the queen. White defends with the knight and the queen. The counts are equal.

items.explain: The pawn on c3 adds a third defender to the knight and the queen, while Black still has only the c-pawn and the queen. The count is two against three, so d4 cannot be won by force.

items.explain: The move a3 does not touch d4, so both counts stay at two. A difference that does not touch the pawn changes nothing.

items.prompt: Black is in check from the bishop. Find the reply that keeps the extra piece and the edge.

claims.statement: At depth 16 the block ...e6 is the best reply.
The bishop block loses at least 500 centipawns more than the best move.
The knight block gives up at least 150 centipawns.

hints: Blocking on the diagonal is one option; see what each block leaves behind.
A pawn can block without being pinned.
The pawn from e7 steps to e6.
items.explain: The pawn goes to e6 and blocks the bishop's diagonal. It opens a diagonal for the f8 bishop and the queen, and it is defended by the c8 bishop and the king. The bishop block on e6 would be pinned to the king; the knight block on d5 allows strong follow-ups and cuts Black's edge to nearly nothing.

feedback_by_move.c8e6: The bishop is now pinned to the king. The knight check on e5 drives the king away and the bishop falls.
feedback_by_move.f6d5: This block is possible but the engine (depth 16) sees the edge shrink to about zero after the queen and knight get to work.
feedback_by_move.f7e8: Retreating instead of blocking leaves the king in the middle and gives White free tempi.
feedback_by_move.f7g6: The king walks into the open; the checks do not stop.

items.prompt: Black is in check from the knight. Which king move keeps the edge?

claims.statement: At depth 16 the king move to g8 is the best reply.
The move to e8 loses at least 300 centipawns.
The move to e6 loses at least 700 centipawns.

hints: The king has three squares: g8, e8 and e6.
Which squares leave the long diagonal of the white bishop and the knight's fork squares?
The corner: the king goes to g8.
items.explain: The king on g8 steps off the diagonal from c4 and out of range of the knight, and it keeps h7 for later. On e8 the king invites the bishop to d3 and g6 with check; on e6 it walks into the open and into the check on the diagonal.

feedback_by_move.f7e8: The bishop swings to d3 and the knight gets the fork square f7: the engine shows a swing of more than three pawns.
feedback_by_move.f7e6: The king walks into the centre: the bishop check on c4 comes with tempo and the engine sees a swing of more than ten pawns.

items.prompt: Black to move. The pawn on e6 is attacked twice and defended twice. Find a good move.

claims.statement: At depth 16 ...cxd4 and ...Nc6 are within 40 centipawns.
After ...Nbd7 White mates in three, starting with the queen capture on e6.
The queen capture on d4 loses at least 500 centipawns.

hints: Count the defenders of e6 after your move.
The bishop on c8 is one of the two defenders.
Capture on d4 with the pawn, or develop the knight to c6.
items.explain: The pawn capture on d4 wins a pawn because the knight is the only white defender of d4. The knight to c6 is just as good. Moving the b8 knight to d7 blocks the bishop's guard of e6: then the queen takes on e6 with check and mates in three. The queen capture on d4 loses the queen to the knight.

feedback_by_move.b8d7: The knight blocks the c8 bishop: e6 loses a defender and Qxe6+ leads to mate in three.
feedback_by_move.d8d4: The queen is taken by the knight: Black has only a knight and pawn for the queen.
feedback_by_move.f7g8: Too slow: White plays Bxe6+ or keeps the initiative.

items.prompt: Black to move. Find a good move (several work).

claims.statement: At depth 16 ...Na5 and ...Nd5 are within 50 centipawns.
The game move ...Bd6 loses at least 400 centipawns.

hints: The rook on e1 looks through the e-file to e6.
Count attackers and defenders of e6 after your move.
Several moves work: Na5 and ...b5 attack the bishop on c4, Nd5 blocks its diagonal, and Qa5 attacks the rook on e1.
items.explain: The rook adds a second attacker to e6, which only the bishop on c8 defends. Black needs a move that keeps the pawn guarded or removes an attacker: ...Na5 or ...b5 attacks the bishop on c4, ...Nd5 blocks the bishop's diagonal, and ...Qa5 hits the rook on e1. The bishop move to d6 allows Rxe6, an exchange sacrifice that works here.

feedback_by_move.f8d6: The game move: e6 is attacked twice and defended once, and Rxe6 works as an exchange sacrifice because the black king is left exposed.
